units.translation: the hoopoe, overseer of his own evils
who has done many evils to me in the house
not to be angry with the gods in misfortunes
not to heal evils with evils
to repay the enemy with evils
death, the greatest deliverance from many evils
so that you may not make the citizens cowardly
you will pass by scanty and ill-spread couches
Schol. causing to be at leisure for evil
and breezes coming from the Strymon, bringing evil leisure
causing to be at leisure for evil
how do you bid me practice wickedness?
thus Hermann for ὃ γοῦν [which indeed], which is in Stobaeus Flor. 125, 7.
if you wish to benefit the dead or to harm them
Explained by the schol. as κακώσει [ill-treatment].
in the unfortunate possession of his fatherland
of anxiety, which now sometimes is fulfilled as ill-boding
when he wishes to ruin a house utterly
the naval army having been maltreated
and by the destruction of the seed of children the vigor is ruined
where Meineke conjectured κατεσποδημένου [having been dashed down].
the army having toiled and being badly dashed down
to speak badly of those who are near
and to me Zeus gave to think not badly
to the one speaking most badly
[with present passive and middle form καλοῦμαι, perfect κέκλημαι, future κεκλήσομαι.] to call, invoke, summon
where, as the meter demands, I wrote δ᾽ ἐπανακαλῶ [and I call upon in addition] Παιᾶνα [Paean]

where κεκλήσεται [will be called] is restored from the copies, as commonly written in Tzetzes on Lycophr. 630. κληθήσεται [will be called] M, as in Tzetzes in the manuscripts. The usual form of the future passive among the ancients is κεκλήσομαι [I will be called], sometimes changed to κληθήσομαι [I will be called] by scribes, as in this verse of Aeschylus and in Eur. Troad. 13, which the ancients rarely, the more recent writers more often use: on which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 4 p. 870.
where the meter excludes the other form.
I call upon the all-seeing circle of the sun
and the empty one calls the empty
again coming to your kindred – he calls
he calls upon the ancestral gods
for you call us, being well-disposed, as counselors of these things
and I call upon the healer
speaking ill-omened words she calls upon the god
this third libation of the house I call
he ordered to call Aegisthus as quickly as possible
calling upon the might of Poseidon
for now I call you a dream, Clytemnestra
I call upon the queen of this land
